title: Could humans live symbiotically with AI?
author: @sfiscience
text:
Researchers explore whether symbiogenesis, in which organisms combine to form new life, offers a useful way to think about humans and AI. (image: Edson De la O/SFI)November 19, 2026Occasionally throughout evolutionary history, multiple organisms have combined to create new forms of life, a turbo-charged form of evolution known as symbiogenesis, an idea with a long and rich history at SFI. Think of prokaryotes being subsumed by others to become eukaryotic cells, or single cells joining together to create multicellular life.

Current narratives around AI focus either on AI dominating humans or on AI as a subservient tool. Could the concept of symbiogenesis be a fruitful alternative framework for thinking about interactions between humans and AI?

An SFI working group titled “Symbiogenesis in the Age of Machine Intelligence” met September 17–18 to explore this hypothesis. The paradigm of symbiogenesis, which has roots in complex systems and evolutionary research, “provides a very different frame in which to consider this possibility that the AI is not just a tool that’s alongside us, but in some sense becomes part of us,” says SFI External Professor James Evans (University of Chicago).

Evans co-organized the working group with SFI External Professor Blaise Agüera y Arcas (Google); Benjamin Bratton of the University of California, San Diego; and Google’s Alice Guan to explore how symbiogenesis might inform how we expect intelligence and institutions to evolve.

AI systems share important qualities with living systems — such as energy, learning, and agency — inspiring the organizers to borrow a framework normally exclusive to biotic life and apply it to biology plus technology. 

“We’re trying to make sense of this moment and to guide technology that enables human prosperity, safety, and flourishing,” Evans explains. The results could lead researchers to rethink AI safety research as well as explore new kinds of complex, symbiogenetic combinations of human and machine intelligence.

The working group comprised a multidisciplinary array of synthetic and evolutionary biologists, philosophers, computer and social scientists, as well as a historian of science fiction. “We wanted to probe this framing from a number of different points of view to see where it’s fruitful for driving AI research and policy forward,” Evans says. The group explored topics such as the history of transitions, artificial life, superorganisms, hybrid systems, and distributed cognition.

The group plans to synthesize its results into a forthcoming position paper. In addition, members are working on funding proposals for several collaborative research projects to explore novel human-AI symbiogenetic “centaur” systems.

Ultimately, the working group demonstrated that “this is a promising way of thinking about and bringing new light and motivation to classic and increasingly stale perspectives on understanding and regulating AI,” Evans says.
